title: The Holy Girl
full_review:
Don't be fooled. Yes, the titular character -- a teenage schoolgirl named Amalia (Maria Alche) is possessed of religious fervor, and she talks endlessly with her girlfriend about vocations -- but this is hardly "The Song of Bernadette."

The opening scene -- a school music class where the soloist sings "What is it Lord, that you want of me?" -- might suggest a traditional spiritual quest is about to unfold.

In fact, "The Holy Girl" (Fine Line) is a tedious and talky Spanish-language film concerning Amalia's pursuit of the married Dr. Jano (Carlos Belloso), after he inappropriately presses up against her in a crowd. Her adolescent mind filled with the pious ideas she's picked up in school, she hits on the notion of "saving" him, though saving in this case seems more like seducing.

Jano does not encourage Amalia's intentions, though he seems slightly tempted. Generally, he seems to be trying to do the "right thing" and shake off the girl.

He does, however, find he's attracted to her divorcee mother, Helena (Mercedes Moran), who runs the hotel where he and other doctors are staying for a medical convention.

Helena's brother, Freddy (Alejandro Urdapilleta), runs the business with her, and thinks nothing of chastely sharing his sister and niece's bed. (In fact, all the characters in "The Holy Girl" spend an awful lot of time reclining next to each other.)

Up-and-coming Argentine writer-director Lucrecia Martel's film is not as sensational as the plot summary might suggest. Martel favors a subtle, nuanced approach, and the sexual tensions are mostly below the surface. There's a little fleeting nudity, courtesy of a couple of secondary characters, and no overt sex at all except for some under-the-covers tussling (presumably nonsexual) between Amalia's friend, Josefina (Julieta Zylberberg), and her boyfriend, and an episode where the two girls kiss, though the brief moment is shown to be more one of adolescent curiosity than passion.

Martel has acknowledged her film was made from the tenuous perspective of her Catholic upbringing; included are the themes of "the dangers of differentiating good from evil," taking "back the reins of our own existence" and "drawing a line between live tissue and moral prosthesis" -- whatever that means!

Though some film buffs may appreciate Martel's artsy filmic style, most viewers will be turned off by the sluggish narrative, mostly unappealing characters and dreary production design. Whatever Catholic underpinning there may be in all this seems inconsequential.

Pedro Almodovar served as one of the film's executive producers. Would that Martel had at least borrowed a bit of his cinematic panache.

The film, with subtitles, contains some fleeting rear and partial nudity, adolescent sexual musings, same-sex kissing and a nonsexual bed scene. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
